        \mathcal{P}_{n,m,\kappa} = \bigcap_{i=1}^m\left\{x \in \mathbb{R}^n\,:\, |\langle x,\, A_i \rangle | \le \kappa\right\}\,.

title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thmStructure}
Fix $\kappa>0$ and $\alpha\in(1,\alpha_c(\kappa))$ such that
\cref{hyp:maxima} holds. Let
$m=\lfloor\alpha n\rfloor$, $\mathcal{Z}=|\mathbf{X}_{n,m,\kappa}|$, and $r_*=r_*(\kappa,\alpha)$. The following hold with high probability:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item\label{item:freezing} (Strong freezing.)
    For some $\delta = \delta(\kappa,\alpha)>0$, almost all solutions $x \in \mathbf{X}_{n,m,\kappa}$ are $\delta$-frozen.

    \item\label{item:typical orthogonal} (Typical pairs of solutions are almost orthogonal)
    Almost all pairs of solutions $(x,y)\in\mathbf{X}_{n,m,\kappa}^2$ satisfy $$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le \sqrt n\log n \,.$$
    
    \item \label{item:typical empirical} (Empirical distribution of a typical solution)
    For almost all  solutions $ x \in \mathbf{X}_{n,m,\kappa} $, $$ \|\nu_x-\mu_{r_*}\|_{\mathrm{TV}} =o(1)\,.$$

    \item \label{item:lognormal} The random variable $\mathcal{Z}/ \mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\mathcal{Z}\right]$ has a log-normal limit (explicitly given in \cref{lem:lognormal}).
\end{enumerate}

title: Remark
body_md: Our parameterization of the discrete Gaussian distribution $\mu_r$ is through its variance $r^2$. In the    computer science literature, especially in lattice cryptography, the discrete Gaussian is often parameterized by $\sigma^2$, the parameter appearing in the exponential. Another parameterization frequently employed in this paper and arising from viewing the discrete Gaussian as an exponential family solving a maximum entropy problem, is to set $a := a(r) = -1/(2\sigma^2)$, $b = -\log Z$, and $\mu_r(\ell) = e^{a \ell^2 +  b}$.

title: Definition
body_md:
For $r\ge1$, define
\[
    \Lambda_n(r):=\left\{x\in\Lambda_n:\|x\|_2^2=nr^2\right\},
    \qquad
    \mathbf{X}(r) := \mathbf{X} \cap\Lambda_n(r),
    \qquad
    \mathcal{Z}_r:=|\mathbf{X}(r)|,
\]
and let
\[
    N_n(r) := |\Lambda_n(r)|, \qquad \mathcal{R}_n:=\left\{r\ge1:\Lambda_n(r)\ne\emptyset\right\}.
\]
For $J\subset[1,\infty)$, set
\[
    \mathcal{Z}_J:=\sum_{r\in J\cap\mathcal{R}_n}\mathcal{Z}_r
    =\left|\bigcup_{r\in J\cap\mathcal{R}_n}
      \mathbf{X}(r)\right|.
\]
We also define an analogous count of lattice pairs. For $r,\hat{r} \in \mathcal{R}_n$ and $\theta \in [-1,1]$ with $\theta r\hat{r} n \in \mathbb{Z}$,
\[
    \Lambda_n(r,\hat{r},\theta):=\left\{(x,y)\in\Lambda_n(r) \times \Lambda_n(\hat{r}): \langle x,y \rangle = \theta r \hat{r} n\right\},
    \qquad
    N_n(r,\hat{r},\theta):= |\Lambda_n(r,\hat{r},\theta)|\,.
\]
head: environment
name: Solution spheres

title: Remark
body_md: A reasonable, but absolutely wrong, low-dimensional intuition is that $N_n(r)$ scales proportionally to the Euclidean volume of the $n$-ball of radius $r\sqrt{n}$ \cite{mazo1990lattice}. The above computations establish that this is off by an exponential factor. The intuition is that the discrepancy between the volume and number of integer points in a body is largely due to boundary effects, whereas almost all of the volume of a high-dimensional sphere lies near its boundary. However, as $r$ diverges, the entropy of $\mu_r$ approaches $\frac12\log(2\pi e r^2)$, the differential entropy of $N(0,r^2)$. For fixed $r$, this also equals the limiting normalized log-volume of the ball, $n^{-1}\log \mathrm{Vol} \,B_n(0,r\sqrt{n})$. Hence, as $r \to 1$ and $r \to \infty$, the integer geometry of our model approaches the discrete cube and continuum respectively, and is non-trivial everywhere in between.

label: lemma:max entropy
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma:max entropy}
Let $\Omega$ be a countable set, let $f:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^d$, and fix
$b\in\mathbb{R}^d$. Suppose that, for some $\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^d$,
\[
    Z:=\sum_{x\in\Omega}e^{\langle\lambda,f(x)\rangle}<\infty,
    \qquad
    \mu(x):=Z^{-1}e^{\langle\lambda,f(x)\rangle}
\]
satisfies $\mathbb{E}_{\mu\unskip\space}\left[f\right]=b$. Then, writing
$\Omega_b:=\{x\in\Omega:f(x)=b\}$ and assuming that this set is finite,
\[
    |\Omega_b|=e^{H(\mu)}\mu(\Omega_b).
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $H(\mu)=\log Z-\langle\lambda,b\rangle$, for $x\in\Omega_b$ one has
$\mu(x)=Z^{-1}e^{\langle\lambda,b\rangle}=e^{-H(\mu)}$. Then $
\mathbb{P}_{\mu}\left[\Omega_b\right] = |\Omega_b|e^{-H(\mu)}$. Rearranging gives the claim.

label: prop:1d-lattice-count
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:1d-lattice-count}
For every $r\ge1$,
\[
    N(r)
    =e^{nH(\mu_r)}
      \mathbb{P}_{X\sim\mu_r^{\otimes n}}\left[\|X\|_2^2=nr^2\right]
    \le e^{nH(\mu_r)}.
\]
Moreover, for every $\delta>0$ and $C<\infty$, uniformly over
$r\in[1+\delta,C]$ such that $nr^2\in\mathbb{Z}$,
\[
    N(r)
    =e^{nH(\mu_r)}
      \frac{1+o(1)}{\sqrt{2\pi n\mathrm{Var}_{\mu_r}(X_1^2)}}
    =\Theta(n^{-1/2})e^{nH(\mu_r)}.
\]
For $r=1$, one has $N(1)=2^n$.
head: environment
name: Asymptotic count of lattice points

title: Proof
body_md:
Apply \cref{lemma:max entropy} with
$\Omega=(\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\})^n$ and $f(x)=\|x\|_2^2$; take $\mu_r^{\otimes n}$ as the distribution $\mu$ in the Lemma, as its log-density is
affine in $f$ and $\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[f\right]=nr^2$. This gives the first identity. The remaining assertion follows from the lattice-valued local central limit theorem \cite[Ch.~5, \S\,22]{lclt}, uniformly when $r$ ranges over a compact subset of $(1,\infty)$. Indeed, in this regime the moments are uniformly bounded, $\mathrm{Var}_{\mu_r}(X_1^2)$ is bounded away from zero, and the lattice span of $X_1^2$ is one.

label: prop:2d-lattice-count
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Asymptotic lattice-pair count

title: Proof
body_md:
Apply \cref{lemma:max entropy} with
\[
    \Omega=((\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\})^2)^n,
    \qquad
    f((x_i,y_i)_{i\le n})=\sum_i(x_i^2,x_iy_i,y_i^2).
\]
The associated distribution is
$(\mu_{r,\hat r,\theta}^{(2)})^{\otimes n}$, which gives the first exact
identity and upper bound. Next, on the compact parameter set, the covariance matrix
$\Gamma_{r,\hat r,\theta}$ is uniformly non-degenerate, all moments are
uniformly bounded, and the lattice generated by differences of support
points is $\mathbb Z^3$. The multivariate lattice local central limit
theorem therefore gives \eqref{eq:2d lattice count}.

Finally, at $\theta=0$, note that
$\mu_{r,\hat r,0}^{(2)}=\mu_r\otimes\mu_{\hat r}$ and
\[
    \det\Gamma_{r,\hat r,0}
    =\mathrm{Var}_{\mu_r}(X^2)\,r^2\hat r^2\,
      \mathrm{Var}_{\mu_{\hat r}}(Y^2).
\]
Taking logarithms in \eqref{eq:2d lattice count}, using
\cref{prop:1d-lattice-count}, and Taylor expanding the two even analytic
functions
$H(\mu_{r,\hat r,\theta}^{(2)})$ and
$\log\det\Gamma_{r,\hat r,\theta}$ at $\theta=0$ gives
\eqref{eq:N2 expansion}.

label: prop:H(DG) properties
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:H(DG) properties}
Let $r>1$ and write $v=v(r):=r^2$. Viewing $H(\mu_r)$ as a function of $v$, one has
\[
    \partial_{vv}^2H(\mu_r)<0<\partial_vH(\mu_r)
\]
and
\[
    -\frac{\partial_vH(\mu_r)}{\partial_{vv}^2H(\mu_r)}
    =\frac1{2\sigma^2}\left(\mathbb{E}_{\mu_r\unskip\space}\left[X^4\right]-v^2\right).
\]
Moreover, as $r\to\infty$,
\[
    \partial_vH(\mu_r)=\frac{1+o(1)}{2r^2},
    \qquad
    H(\mu_r)=\log r+O(1).
\]
head: environment
name: Entropy of the discrete Gaussian

label: eq:relations-mu_r
title: Proof
body_md:
Set $a:=a(v)$ and $b:=b(v)$, with
\[
    \mu_r(x)=e^{ax^2+b}.
\]
Thus $a=-1/(2\sigma^2)$ and $b=-\log Z$. The relations
\begin{equation}\label{eq:relations-mu_r}
    v=\sum_xe^{ax^2+b}x^2,
    \qquad
    1=\sum_xe^{ax^2+b}
\end{equation}
give $a'v+b'=0$. Since $H(\mu_r)=-(av+b)$,
\[
    -\partial_vH(\mu_r)=a,
    \qquad
    -\partial_{vv}^2H(\mu_r)=a'.
\]
Here $a<0$, while differentiating the first identity in
\eqref{eq:relations-mu_r} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:implicitdiff-mu_r}
    1=a'\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[X^4\right]+b'v.
\end{equation}
Combining this with $a'v+b'=0$ gives
\[
    1=a'\left(\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[X^4\right]-v^2\right).
\]
Hence, $a'>0$. It follows that
\[
    -\frac{\partial_vH(\mu_r)}{\partial_{vv}^2H(\mu_r)}
    =-\frac a{a'}
    =-a\left(\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[X^4\right]-v^2\right)
    =\frac1{2\sigma^2}\left(\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[X^4\right]-v^2\right).
\]

For the asymptotics, let $t:=-a=1/(2\sigma^2)$. By Poisson summation,
\[
    Z(t):=2\sum_{k\ge1}e^{-tk^2}
    =\sqrt{\frac\pi t}\left(1+O(e^{-\pi^2/t})\right)-1.
\]
Hence
\[
    r^2=-\frac{d}{dt}\log Z(t)
    =\frac1{2t}\left(1+O(\sqrt t)\right).
\]
Since $\partial_vH(\mu_r)=t$, the first asymptotic follows. The identity
$H(\mu_r)=tr^2+\log Z(t)$ then gives $H(\mu_r)=\log r+O(1)$.

label: prop:DG moments
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:DG moments}
Let $X\sim\mu_r$, where $\mu_r$ is the punctured discrete Gaussian with variance $r^2$. For all $r>1$,
\[
    \frac1{2\sigma^2}\left(\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[X^4\right]-r^4\right)<r^2.
\]
head: environment
name: Discrete Gaussian moment inequality

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $t=1/(2\sigma^2)$, and define
\[
    Z(t)=2\sum_{j\ge1}e^{-tj^2},
    \qquad
    R(t)=-\frac{d}{dt}\log Z(t).
\]
Then $R(t)=r^2$, $R'(t)=-\mathrm{Var}(X^2)$, and the desired inequality is
equivalent to $(tR(t))'>0$.
First, consider $0<t\le1/2$. Poisson summation gives
\[
    Z(t)=\bigl(\sqrt{\pi/t}-1\bigr)(1+\delta(t)),
    \qquad
    \delta(t)=
    \frac{2\sum_{m\ge1}e^{-\pi^2m^2/t}}{1-\sqrt{t/\pi}},
\]
and hence
\[
    tR(t)=\frac12+\frac1{2(\sqrt{\pi/t}-1)}
           -t\frac{d}{dt}\log(1+\delta(t)).
\]
The derivative of the first two terms is greater than $.53$ for $0 < t \le 1/2$, using the standard truncation formulas for geometric series. On the other hand, differentiating and using the inequality
$m^2\ge1+3(m-1)$ gives an absolute bound of, e.g., $10^{-4}$ for the
derivative of the last term. Hence $(tR(t))' > .5 > 0$, as desired. 

It remains to consider $t\ge1/2$. Let $Y=X^2-1$. Since
$\mathrm{Var}(Y)\le\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[Y^2\right]$,
\[
    (tR(t))'
    \ge
    \frac{1+\sum_{j\ge2}
       \bigl((j^2-1)-t(j^2-1)^2\bigr)e^{-t(j^2-1)}}
         {1+\sum_{j\ge2}e^{-t(j^2-1)}}.
\]
Keeping the terms $j=2,3$ and bounding the remaining geometric tail,
the numerator is at least
\[
    1+(3-9t)e^{-3t}+(8-64t)e^{-8t}-300te^{-15t}
    >1-3e^{-2}-24e^{-4}-150e^{-15/2}>0.
\]
Thus $(tR(t))' > 0$ for $t \ge 1/2$, completing the proof of the proposition in all cases.

label: cor:F1 unique max
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:F1 unique max}
Fix $\kappa>0$ and $\alpha>1$. There exist a unique
$r_*\in(1,\infty)$ and constants $c,c'>0$, depending only on $\kappa$ and $\alpha$, such that for all $r\ge1$,
\[
    F_1(\kappa,\alpha,r)
    \le F_1(\kappa,\alpha,r_*)-
       \min\{c',c|r-r_*|^2\}.
\]
head: environment
name: Unique maximum for first moment

title: Proof
body_md:
We first prove the dichotomy. In what follows, primes denote derivatives with respect to $v=r^2$. A computation gives
\[
    \partial_{vv}^2\log p(\kappa/r)
    =-\frac{\kappa e^{-\kappa^2/r^2}
      \left(\sqrt{2\pi}e^{\kappa^2/(2r^2)}(\kappa^2-3r^2)p(\kappa/r)
      +2\kappa r\right)}
      {4\pi r^7p(\kappa/r)^2},
\]
which is strictly negative for $r\le\kappa/2$.

Fix $v$ and suppose that $f''(v)\ge0$. Then necessarily $r>\kappa/2$ and
\[
    \partial_{vv}^2\log p(\kappa/r)
    \ge-\frac1\alpha\partial_{vv}^2H(\mu_r)>0.
\]
Also,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:E1}
    \partial_v\log p(\kappa/r)
    =-\frac{\kappa e^{-\kappa^2/(2r^2)}}
      {\sqrt{2\pi}r^3p(\kappa/r)}<0.
\end{equation}
Thus it is enough to show
\begin{equation}\label{eq:dichotomy goal}
    \frac{H(\mu_r)'(\log p(\kappa/r))''}
         {H(\mu_r)''(\log p(\kappa/r))'}<1.
\end{equation}
A direct computation yields
\[
    \frac{(\log p(\kappa/r))''}{(\log p(\kappa/r))'}
    =\frac1{r^2}\left(
       \frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}\frac\kappa r
       \frac{e^{-\kappa^2/(2r^2)}}{p(\kappa/r)}
       +\frac{\kappa^2}{2r^2}-\frac32\right).
\]
The left-hand side is negative under our assumption. Using
$p(x)\le x\sqrt{2/\pi}$ and $e^{-x^2/2}\ge1-x^2/2$, we obtain
\[
    \left|\frac{(\log p(\kappa/r))''}{(\log p(\kappa/r))'}\right|
    \le\frac1{r^2}\left(1-\frac{\kappa^2}{4r^2}\right).
\]
On the other hand, \cref{prop:H(DG) properties,prop:DG moments} give
\[
    \left|\frac{H(\mu_r)'}{H(\mu_r)''}\right|
    =\frac1{2\sigma^2}\left(\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[X^4\right]-r^4\right)<r^2.
\]
Combining the last two displays proves \eqref{eq:dichotomy goal}, and hence the dichotomy.

We next show that $f'(v)>0$ near $v=1$. Write
$\mu_r(x)=e^{ax^2+b}$ and let $q=\mathbb{P}_{}\left[|X|>1\right]$. Since
$v\ge1+3q$, one has $q\to0$ as $v\downarrow1$, while
\[
    e^{3a}=\frac{\mathbb{P}_{}\left[|X|=2\right]}{\mathbb{P}_{}\left[|X|=1\right]}\le\frac q{1-q}.
\]
Thus $a\to-\infty$. Since $\partial_vH(\mu_r)=-a$ and
$\partial_v\log p(\kappa/r)$ remains bounded, $f'(v)>0$ near $1$.
Finally, \cref{prop:H(DG) properties} and \eqref{eq:E1} give, as
$r\to\infty$,
\[
    f'(v)=\frac{1-\alpha+o(1)}{2r^2}<0.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $f$ be as in \cref{lemma:F1 shape}. Since $f'>0$ near $1$ and
$f'<0$ eventually,
\[
    v_*:=\inf\{v>1:f'(v)\le0\}
\]
is finite, satisfies $v_*>1$, and obeys $f'(v_*)=0$. The dichotomy gives
$f''(v_*)<0$, so $f'<0$ immediately to the right of $v_*$. If $f'$ returned to zero, let $w>v_*$ be its first subsequent zero. Then
$f'<0$ on $(v_*,w)$, and hence $f''(w)\ge0$, contradicting the dichotomy. Therefore $f'>0$ on $(1,v_*)$ and $f'<0$ on $(v_*,\infty)$, so $v_*$ is the unique maximizer.

Since $f''(v_*)<0$, there are $c_0,\delta>0$ such that
\[
    f(v)\le f(v_*)-c_0(v-v_*)^2
    \qquad\text{for }|v-v_*|\le\delta.
\]
Monotonicity on either side of $v_*$ gives a constant $c_1>0$ such that
$f(v)\le f(v_*)-c_1$ whenever $|v-v_*|\ge\delta$. Writing
$v=r^2$ and $v_*=r_*^2$ now gives the claimed global estimate.
head: environment

label: eq:F1-capacity-sign
title: Remark
body_md:
Recall that 
\[
    \alpha_c(\kappa) := \sup_{r\ge 1} \frac{H(\mu_r)}{-\log p(\kappa/r)}\,.
\]
It is a minor subtlety that, \textit{a priori}, the supremum in this definition may only be attained in the limit as $r$ diverges so that $F_1(\kappa,\alpha_c(\kappa),r)$ could potentially be negative for every finite $r$. This is a danger if the margin $\kappa$ is extremely small, so that the model goes from almost surely having infinite solutions when $\alpha < 1$ and $A$ has a kernel, to suddenly having no solutions when $\alpha = 1$. Fortunately, this turns out to be the only obstruction: the supremum is attained as long as $\alpha_c(\kappa)>1$. A Taylor expansion gives
\[
    p(\kappa/r)
    =\sqrt{\frac2\pi}\,\frac{\kappa}{r}+O(r^{-3}).
\]
Combining this estimate with \cref{prop:H(DG) properties}, we have $-H(\mu_r)/\log p(\kappa/r) \to 1$ as $r \to \infty$. In particular, $\alpha_c(\kappa)\ge1$. Thus, if $\alpha_c(\kappa)>1$, continuity of $H(\mu_r)/\log p(\kappa/r)$ implies that the supremum above is attained at some finite $r$. Together with \cref{cor:F1 unique max}, we have for $\alpha>1$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:F1-capacity-sign}
    \max_{r\ge1}F_1(\kappa,\alpha,r)
    =
    \begin{cases}
        >0, & \alpha<\alpha_c(\kappa),\\
        0,  & \alpha=\alpha_c(\kappa),\\
        <0, & \alpha>\alpha_c(\kappa).
    \end{cases}
\end{equation}
head: environment
name: Capacity

title: Proof
body_md:
The existence and uniqueness of $r_*$ follow from
\cref{cor:F1 unique max}. Write
\[F_1(r):=F_1(\kappa,\alpha,r), \qquad  F_*:=F_1(r_*).\]
Throughout the proof, $c,C>0$ denote constants depending only on
$(\kappa,\alpha)$ which may change from line to line.

We first control the infinity norm. For all sufficiently large $n$, the interval $I$ lies in a fixed compact subset of $(1,\infty)$. Uniformly over $r\in I$, \cref{prop:1d-lattice-count} gives
\[
    \mathbb{P}_{X\sim\mu_r^{\otimes n}}\left[\|X\|_2^2=nr^2\right]=\Theta(n^{-1/2}).
\]
Writing $\mu_r(x)\propto e^{a(r)x^2}$, continuity gives $a(r)\le-c<0$ uniformly on this compact set. A union bound gives
\[
    \mathbb{P}_{X\sim\mu_r^{\otimes n}}\left[\|X\|_\infty>\log n\right]
    \le e^{-c(\log n)^2}.
\]
Since the uniform measure on $\Lambda_n(r)$ is exactly 
$\mu_r^{\otimes n}$ conditioned on $\{\|X\|_2^2=nr^2\}$, it follows that
\[
    |\Lambda_n(r)\setminus\Lambda_n^\text{\tiny{typ}}(r)| \le |\Lambda_n(r)|\, \frac{\mathbb{P}_{X\sim\mu_r^{\otimes n}}\left[\|X\|_\infty>\log n\right]}{\mathbb{P}_{X\sim\mu_r^{\otimes n}}\left[\|X\|_2^2=nr^2\right]}
    \le e^{-c(\log n)^2}|\Lambda_n(r)|.
\]
Rotational invariance of the Gaussian constraints therefore gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:E[Z] - typical}
    \mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\mathcal{Z}_I-\mathcal{Z}_I^\text{\tiny{typ}}\right]
    \le e^{-c(\log n)^2}\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\mathcal{Z}_I\right],
    \qquad
    \mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\mathcal{Z}_I\right]
    =\left(1+O(e^{-c(\log n)^2})\right)\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\mathcal{Z}_I^\text{\tiny{typ}}\right].
\end{equation}

It remains to truncate the radius. For sufficiently
large $n$, the uniform local central limit
theorem and a Taylor expansion of $F_1$ around $r_*$ give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:lower bound EZ I}
    \mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\mathcal{Z}_I\right]\ge c\,e^{nF_*}.
\end{equation}

Fix $\delta\in(0,r_*-1)$. For $|r-r_*|\le\delta$, the local central
limit theorem and \cref{cor:F1 unique max} give
\[
    \mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\mathcal{Z}_r\right]
    \le Cn^{-1/2}e^{nF_*}e^{-cn(r-r_*)^2}.
\]
Writing $q:=nr^2$ and $q_*:=nr_*^2$, we have in this range
\[
    n(r-r_*)^2=\frac{(q-q_*)^2}{n(r+r_*)^2}
    \ge c\frac{(q-q_*)^2}{n}.
\]
Summing the resulting Gaussian tail over $q\in\mathbb Z$ yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:F1 trunc mid}
    \sum_{\substack{r\in\mathcal{R}_n\setminus I\\|r-r_*|\le\delta}}
        \mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\mathcal{Z}_r\right]
    \le e^{-cw_n^2}\,\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\mathcal{Z}_I\right].
\end{equation}

Fix a sufficiently large constant $R>r_*+\delta$. By continuity and uniqueness of the maximizer,
$F_1(r)\le F_*-c$ when $r\in[1,R]$ and $|r-r_*|>\delta$. The exact counting identity in
\cref{prop:1d-lattice-count} gives
$\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\mathcal{Z}_r\right]\le e^{nF_1(r)}$, and there are only $O(n)$ possible values of $nr^2$ in this bounded range. Hence
\[
    \sum_{\substack{r\in\mathcal{R}_n\cap[1,R]\\|r-r_*|>\delta}}
        \mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\mathcal{Z}_r\right]
    \le e^{-cn}\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\mathcal{Z}_I\right].
\]
Finally, \cref{prop:H(DG) properties} and
$p(\kappa/r)\le\sqrt{2/\pi}\,\kappa/r$ imply, for $r$ sufficiently large,
\[
    \mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\mathcal{Z}_r\right]\le\left(C_{\kappa,\alpha}r^{1-\alpha}\right)^n.
\]
Grouping the possible values of $nr^2$ according to $k\le r<k+1$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:F1 trunc extreme}
    \sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}_n:\,r\ge R}\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\mathcal{Z}_r\right]
    \le\sum_{k\ge R}n(2k+1)
       \left(C_{\kappa,\alpha}k^{1-\alpha}\right)^n
    \le e^{-cn}\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\mathcal{Z}_I\right],
\end{equation}
where $R$ is chosen sufficiently large and we used $F_*\ge0$ from \eqref{eq:F1-capacity-sign}, together with \eqref{eq:lower bound EZ I}. Combining the above computations gives
\[
    \mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\mathcal{Z}-\mathcal{Z}_I\right]
    \le e^{-cw_n^2}\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\mathcal{Z}_I\right].
\]
Together with \eqref{eq:E[Z] - typical}, this proves
\eqref{eq:F1 dominated by r*}. Applying Markov's inequality also yields
\[
    \mathbb{P}_{}\left[0\le\mathcal{Z}-\mathcal{Z}_I^\text{\tiny{typ}}
        \le e^{-cw_n^2}\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\mathcal{Z}_I^\text{\tiny{typ}}\right]\right]
    \ge1-e^{-cw_n^2}.
\]

Finally, let $\alpha$ range over a compact subset of
$(1,\alpha_c(\kappa)]$. Recalling the strict inequality
\[
    \left.\partial_{vv}^2F_1(\kappa,\alpha,\sqrt v)
    \right|_{v=r_*^2}<0,
\]
the implicit function theorem implies that $r_*(\kappa,\alpha)$ is continuous in $\alpha$ and hence ranges over
a compact subset of $(1,\infty)$. Thus, the local central limit theorem,
curvature, compactness, and tail estimates above may be chosen uniformly.

title: Proposition
body_md: Let $r,\hat{r} \in I$ and $\theta \in (-1,1)$. If $\Lambda_n^\text{\tiny{typ}}(r,\hat{r},\theta)\neq \emptyset$, then for all $n$ sufficiently large, \eqref{eq:dg2-condition} is satisfied.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If $r=\hat r$, then \eqref{eq:dg2-condition} is immediate, so assume $r \neq \hat{r}$. Assume without loss of generality that $\theta \in [0,1)$ and then fix some
$(x,y)\in\Lambda_n^\text{\tiny{typ}}(r,\hat{r},\theta)$. Since the coordinates of $x$ and $y$ are integers of absolute
value at most $\log n$,
\begin{align*}
    |r^2-\hat r^2|
    \le\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n|x_i-y_i|\,|x_i+y_i|&\le\frac{2\log n}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n|x_i-y_i| \le 2\log n\,(r^2+\hat r^2-2r\hat r\theta).
\end{align*}
Here we used $|k|\le k^2$ for every integer $k$.
By \cref{sec:1profile}, $r_*$ stays in a compact subset of
$(1,\infty)$. Since $r,\hat r\in I$,
\[
    \log n\,|r^2-\hat r^2|
    =O\left(\frac{\log n\log\log n}{\sqrt n}\right)=o(1).
\]
Consequently, uniformly in these parameters, for all sufficiently
large $n$,
\begin{align*}
    \left(\sqrt{r^2-1}-\sqrt{\hat r^2-1}\right)^2
    =\frac{(r^2-\hat r^2)^2}
        {\left(\sqrt{r^2-1}+\sqrt{\hat r^2-1}\right)^2} &<\frac{|r^2-\hat r^2|}{2\log n} \le r^2+\hat r^2-2r\hat r\theta.
\end{align*}
Rearranging gives \eqref{eq:dg2-condition} as required.

name: Entropy derivatives

title: Proof
body_md:
Let
\[
    T(x,y)=(x^2,xy,y^2),\qquad
    m(\theta)=(r^2,\theta r\hat r,\hat r^2),
\]
and write
\[
    \mathbf a(\theta)=(a(\theta),b(\theta),c(\theta)),
    \qquad
    h(\theta)=H(\mu^{(2)}_{r,\hat r,\theta}).
\]
Differentiating the log-partition function gives
\[
    \nabla\Psi(\mathbf a)=\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[T(X,Y)\right]=m(\theta),
    \qquad
    \nabla^2\Psi(\mathbf a)
      =\mathrm{Cov}(T(X,Y))
      =\Gamma_{r,\hat r,\theta}.
\]
We claim that this covariance matrix is positive definite. Indeed, for
$u=(u_1,u_2,u_3)\in\mathbb{R}^3$,
\[
    u^\top\Gamma_{r,\hat r,\theta}u
      =\mathrm{Var}\bigl(u_1X^2+u_2XY+u_3Y^2\bigr).
\]
If this vanished for some $u\ne0$, then since the law has full support on
$(\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\})^2$, the polynomial
$u_1x^2+u_2xy+u_3y^2$ would be constant there. Fixing $y=1$ and varying
$x$ gives $u_1=u_2=0$, after which varying $y$ gives $u_3=0$, a
contradiction. 

Since
\[
    \log\mu^{(2)}_{r,\hat r,\theta}(x,y)
      =\mathbf a(\theta)\cdot T(x,y)-\Psi(\mathbf a(\theta)),
\]
we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:entropy-Legendre}
    h(\theta)
      =\Psi(\mathbf a(\theta))
         -\mathbf a(\theta)\cdot m(\theta)
      =\inf_{\mathbf u:\,\Psi(\mathbf u)<\infty}
         \{\Psi(\mathbf u)-\mathbf u\cdot m(\theta)\}.
\end{equation}
The infimum is uniquely attained at $\mathbf u=\mathbf a(\theta)$ since
the gradient of the expression being minimized is
$\nabla\Psi(\mathbf u)-m(\theta)$ and its Hessian is positive definite. Differentiating the attained infimum in \eqref{eq:entropy-Legendre} and using
$\nabla\Psi(\mathbf a)=m(\theta)$, we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
    h'(\theta)
      &=\nabla\Psi(\mathbf a)\cdot\mathbf a'
        -\mathbf a'\cdot m(\theta)
        -\mathbf a\cdot m'(\theta) =-\mathbf a\cdot m'(\theta)
       =-b(\theta)r\hat r,
\end{aligned}
\]
which proves \eqref{eq:H-prime}. Differentiating
$m(\theta)=\nabla\Psi(\mathbf a(\theta))$ gives
\[
    m'(\theta)=\Gamma_{r,\hat r,\theta}\mathbf a'(\theta).
\]
Since $m'(\theta)=(0,r\hat r,0)$ is constant,
\[
    h''(\theta)
      =-\mathbf a'(\theta)\cdot m'(\theta)
      =-m'(\theta)^\top
         \Gamma_{r,\hat r,\theta}^{-1}m'(\theta)<0.
\]
This proves that the entropy is strictly concave. Moreover, as $\mu_{r,\hat{r},0}^{(2)}= \mu_r\otimes\mu_{\hat r}$, independence yields \eqref{eq:H''}:
\[
    h''(0)
      =-(r\hat r)^2
        \bigl(\Gamma_{r,\hat r,0}^{-1}\bigr)_{22}
      = - (r\hat{r})^2 \, \mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[X^2Y^2\right]^{-1} 
      =-1. \qedhere
\]

label: eq:energy_derivative
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\varphi_\theta$ denote the density of a pair of standard Gaussian random variables with covariance $\theta$.  Direct differentiation yields
\[
    \partial_\theta\varphi_\theta(x,y) =\partial_x\partial_y\varphi_\theta(x,y).
\]
Integrating this identity over $[-u,u]\times[-v,v]$, and then dividing by $p^{(2)}(u,v,\theta)$, gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:energy_derivative}
\begin{split}
    \partial_\theta\log p^{(2)}(u,v,\theta)
    =\frac{1}{\pi p^{(2)}(u,v,\theta)\sqrt{1-\theta^2}} \left(\exp\left(-\frac{u^2-2\theta uv+v^2}{2(1-\theta^2)}\right)-\exp\left(-\frac{u^2+2\theta uv+v^2}{2(1-\theta^2)}\right)\right).
\end{split}
\end{equation}
In particular,
\[
    \left.\partial_{\theta\theta}^2
      \log p^{(2)}(u,v,\theta)\right|_{\theta=0}
    =d(u)d(v).
\]
Combining this with \eqref{eq:H''}, the result follows.

label: eq:bulk-scalar-estimate
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\overline\Phi(K)=\mathbb{P}_{}\left[W>K\right]$, so that $2\overline\Phi(K) = \mathbb{P}_{}\left[|W|>K\right]= 1-p(K)$. Using \eqref{eq:Gaussian-Hermite-coarse}, the definition of $d(K)$, and the fact that
$\overline\Phi(K)\le\phi(K)/K$, we obtain
\[
    \frac{q(r)}{d(K)}G_K(\theta)
      \le q(r)\frac{\overline\Phi(K)}{K\phi(K)}\theta^2
      \le\frac{q(r)}{K^2}\theta^2.
\]
For the parameter range assumed in the lemma, we verify the scalar estimate
\begin{equation}\label{eq:bulk-scalar-estimate}
    \frac{q(r)}{K^2}
       <\frac{1-1.1/Z_r}{2}
\end{equation}
in
\cref{app:finite-profile-estimates}.  The inequality $D_r(\theta) > \frac{q(r)}{d(K)} G_K(\theta)$ then follows from
\eqref{eq:entropy-interpolation}. Furthermore, \eqref{eq:F2-center}, the positive quadratic gap, and \eqref{eq:F1-stationarity-B} give $q(r)d(K)<1$.

head: environment
name: Near-binary profile

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\kappa\geq 10$, we have $p(\kappa)>.99$, so
\[
    F_1(\kappa,1+\kappa^{-2},1)
      =\log2+(1+\kappa^{-2})\log p(\kappa)>0,
\]
and hence $\alpha_c(\kappa)>1+\kappa^{-2}$. Fix $\alpha$ in the range \eqref{eq:profile-main-range}.
Let $r=r_*(\kappa,\alpha)$ and $K=\kappa/r$. By \eqref{eq:F1-stationarity-B} and
\eqref{eq:F1-capacity-sign}, respectively,
\[
    \alpha=\frac{q(r)}{d(K)},
    \qquad
    F_1(\kappa,\alpha,r)\ge0.
\]
By evenness, it is enough to consider $0<\theta<1$. If $r\ge1.2$ and $K\ge2$, apply
\cref{lem:bulk-profile}. If $K\le2$, then $r\ge5$, and
\eqref{eq:profile-main-range} gives
\[
    \frac{q(r)}{d(K)}=\alpha
       \ge1+\frac1{\kappa^2}
       =1+\frac1{r^2K^2},
\]
so \cref{lem:small-window-profile} applies. The only remaining case is
$1<r<1.2$, which is handled by \cref{lem:near-binary-profile} (noting that the condition $H(\mu_r)+\frac{q(r)}{d(K)}\log p(K) \geq 0$ is equivalent to $F_1(\kappa, \alpha, r) \geq 0$). Thus, in all cases, \eqref{eq:profile-gap} is strictly positive for
$0<\theta<1$, and $1-4B_K^2=1-q(r)d(K)>0$, completing the proof.

title: Definition
body_md:
For $k\ge1$, define the $2k$-cycle count of the first $m$ rows of a
matrix $M$ by
\[
    C_k(m,M):=(nm)^{-k/2}
    \sum_{\substack{i_1,\ldots,i_k\in[n]\ \mathrm{distinct}\\
                    j_1,\ldots,j_k\in[m]\ \mathrm{distinct}}}
    \prod_{\ell=1}^k M_{j_\ell,i_\ell}M_{j_\ell,i_{\ell+1}}
    -\mathbbm{1}_{\{k=1\}}\sqrt{mn},
\]
where $i_{k+1}:=i_1$. Also define
\[
    Y_T(m,M,a):=
    \sum_{k=1}^T
    \frac{2(2B_{a,m/n})^k C_k(m,M)-(2B_{a,m/n})^{2k}}{4k}.
\]

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma:joint normal limits}
There is a sufficiently small $\lambda>0$ such that the following holds.
Let $T=\lfloor\lambda\log n\rfloor$, let $r,\hat r\in I$, and suppose
$|\theta|\le n^{-1/2}\log n$. Uniformly over
$x\in\Lambda_n^{\text{\tiny{typ}}}(r)$ and
$(x,y)\in\Lambda_n^{\text{\tiny{typ}}}(r,\hat r,\theta)$, for every
$g\in\mathcal C^3(\mathbb{R}^T)$ and $W_T\sim N(0,I_T)$,
\begin{align}
    \left|\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[g(V(G))\right]-\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[g(W_T)\right]\right|
    &\le 3n^{-1/5}\sum_{s=1}^3M_s(g),
        \label{eq:joint normal null}\\
    \left|\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[g(V(G)-\rho_r)\mid x\in\mathbf{X}\right]-\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[g(W_T)\right]\right|
    &\le 3n^{-1/5}\sum_{s=1}^3M_s(g),
        \label{eq:joint normal x}\\
    \left|\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[g(V(G)-\rho_r-\rho_{\hat r})\mid x,y\in\mathbf{X}\right]-\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[g(W_T)\right]\right|
    &\le 3n^{-1/5}\sum_{s=1}^3M_s(g).
        \label{eq:joint normal xy}
\end{align}

name: Distribution limits of shifted cycle counts

label: prop:cycle-shifts
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:cycle-shifts}
After decreasing $\lambda>0$ if necessary, uniformly for the parameters
in \cref{lemma:joint normal limits} and $1\le k\le T$,
\begin{align}
    \mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[C_k(m,G^{(x)}+\tau^{(x)})-C_k(m,G)\right]
    &=(2B_{\kappa/r,\alpha})^k+\widetilde O(n^{-1}),
        \label{eq:cycles-x-mean}\\
    \mathrm{Var}\left(C_k(m,G^{(x)}+\tau^{(x)})-C_k(m,G)\right)
    &\le n^{-3/4}\mathrm{Var}\left(C_k(m,G)\right),
        \label{eq:cycles-x-var}\\
    \mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[C_k(m,G^{(x,y)}+\tau^{(x,y)})-C_k(m,G)\right]
    &=(2B_{\kappa/r,\alpha})^k+(2B_{\kappa/\hat r,\alpha})^k
      +\widetilde O(n^{-1}),
        \label{eq:cycles-xy-mean}\\
    \mathrm{Var}\left(C_k(m,G^{(x,y)}+\tau^{(x,y)})-C_k(m,G)\right)
    &\le n^{-3/4}\mathrm{Var}\left(C_k(m,G)\right).
        \label{eq:cycles-xy-var}
\end{align}
Moreover, for $k \ge 2$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:null cycle variance}
    \mathrm{Var}(C_1(m,G))=2,
    \qquad
    \mathrm{Var}(C_k(m,G))
    =2k\frac{(m)_k(n)_k}{m^kn^k}
    =2k\left(1+O\left(\frac{k^2}{m}+\frac{k^2}{n}\right)\right).
\end{equation}

name: Conditional cycle counts

title: Proof
body_md:
The null estimate \eqref{eq:joint normal null} is
given by the proof of \cite[Proposition~3.7]{ss}. That proof applies
verbatim when $m/n$ ranges over a fixed compact subset of
$(0,\infty)$ and $T\le\lambda\log n$, provided $\lambda>0$ is
sufficiently small.

For the one-planted estimate, couple the null matrix as
$G=G^{(x)}+\tau^{(0)}$ and define
\[
    \Delta^{(x)}:=V(G^{(x)}+\tau^{(x)})-\rho_r-V(G).
\]
By \cref{prop:cycle-shifts} and \eqref{eq:null cycle variance},
\[
    \mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\|\Delta^{(x)}\|_2^2\right]
    =\left\|\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\Delta^{(x)}\right]\right\|_2^2
      +\sum_{k=1}^T\mathrm{Var}(\Delta_k^{(x)})
    \le n^{-2/3}
\]
for all sufficiently large $n$. Consequently,
\[
    \left|\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[g(V(G^{(x)}+\tau^{(x)})-\rho_r)\right]-\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[g(V(G))\right]\right|
    \le M_1(g)\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\|\Delta^{(x)}\|_2\right]
    \le M_1(g)n^{-1/3}.
\]
Combining this with \eqref{eq:joint normal null} and
\eqref{eq:one planted coupling} proves \eqref{eq:joint normal x}. The
pair-planted estimate is proven identically, using
\eqref{eq:two planted coupling} in place of \eqref{eq:one planted coupling}.

label: lem:low-rank-cycle-resampling
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:low-rank-cycle-resampling}
Fix $d\le2$. Let $U\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$ satisfy $U^\top U=I_d$ and
$\mu(U)\le n^{-1/2}$. Let $G_j^\perp$, $j\in[m]$, be iid
$N(0,I_n-UU^\top)$ vectors. Independently, let
$\xi_j^{(0)}\sim N(0,I_d)$ and let $\xi_j^{(1)}$ be iid centered random
vectors such that, for some $K<\infty$,
\[
    \sup_{\|v\|_2=1}\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[|\langle v,\xi_j^{(1)}\rangle|^4\right]\le K.
\]
Set
\[
    M_j^{(b)}:=G_j^\perp+U\xi_j^{(b)},
    \qquad
    \Sigma:=\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\xi_j^{(1)}(\xi_j^{(1)})^\top\right],
    \qquad
    D:=\sqrt{m/n}\,(\Sigma-I_d).
\]
There is a constant $C$, depending only on $K$ and the compact range of
$m/n$, such that, uniformly for
$1\le k\le\lambda\log n$,
\begin{align}
    \mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[C_k(m,M^{(1)})-C_k(m,M^{(0)})\right]
    &=\mathrm{tr}(D^k)
      +O\left(k^2\left(\mu(U)+m^{-1}\right)\|D\|_{\mathrm{op}}^k\right),
        \label{eq:low rank mean}\\
    \mathrm{Var}\left(C_k(m,M^{(1)})-C_k(m,M^{(0)})\right)
    &\le C^k k^C\left(\mu(U)+m^{-1}\right)
      \mathrm{Var}(C_k(m,M^{(0)})).
        \label{eq:low rank variance}
\end{align}
head: environment
name: Cycle counts under low-rank resampling

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $u_i:=U^\top e_i$ and $Q:=\Sigma-I_d$. Since
$M^{(0)}$ is an iid standard Gaussian matrix, its cycle counts are
centered. For $k=1$, direct calculation gives
\[
    \mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[C_1(m,M^{(1)})-C_1(m,M^{(0)})\right]
    =\sqrt{m/n}\,\mathrm{tr} Q=\mathrm{tr} D.
\]
For $k\ge2$, the row indices in a cycle are distinct, and the two column
indices incident to each row are distinct. Row independence therefore
gives
\begin{align*}
    \mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[C_k(m,M^{(1)})\right]
    &=\frac{(m)_k}{(mn)^{k/2}}
      \sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_k\ \mathrm{distinct}}
      \prod_{\ell=1}^k u_{i_\ell}^\top Q u_{i_{\ell+1}}.
\end{align*}
Without the distinctness restriction, the sum is $\mathrm{tr}(Q^k)$. To see
the cost of the restriction, fix $1\le a<b\le k$ and impose
$i_a=i_b$. Summing successively over the remaining column indices along
the two arcs from $a$ to $b$ gives
\[
    \sum_{i=1}^n
       (u_i^\top Q^{b-a}u_i)
       (u_i^\top Q^{k-b+a}u_i).
\]
The absolute value of this expression is at most
\[
    \|Q\|_{\mathrm{op}}^k\sum_{i=1}^n\|u_i\|_2^4
    \le d\,\mu(U)\|Q\|_{\mathrm{op}}^k.
\]
There are $O(k^2)$ possible equalities among the column indices.
Excluding them and using $(m)_k/m^k=1+O(k^2/m)$ proves
\eqref{eq:low rank mean}.

We next prove \eqref{eq:low rank variance}. Suppose first that $k\ge2$.
For distinct tuples $\mathbf{i}=(i_1,\ldots,i_k)$ and
$\mathbf{j}=(j_1,\ldots,j_k)$, write
\[
    P_b(\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j})
    :=\prod_{\ell=1}^k
       M^{(b)}_{j_\ell,i_\ell}M^{(b)}_{j_\ell,i_{\ell+1}},
    \qquad i_{k+1}:=i_1,
\]
and let
\[
    \overline P(\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j})
    :=P_1(\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j})-P_0(\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j})
      -\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[P_1(\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j})-P_0(\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j})\right].
\]
Then, writing $Z_k:=C_k(m,M^{(1)})-C_k(m,M^{(0)})$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:low rank variance expansion}
    \mathrm{Var}(Z_k)
    =\frac1{(mn)^k}
      \sum_{\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j},\mathbf{i}',\mathbf{j}'}
      \mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\overline P(\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j})\overline P(\mathbf{i}',\mathbf{j}')\right],
\end{equation}
where each of the four tuples is restricted to have distinct entries.

We estimate this sum by expanding every matrix entry as
\[
    M^{(b)}_{j,i}=G^\perp_{j,i}+u_i^\top\xi_j^{(b)}.
\]
The term using $G^\perp$ at all $2k$ edges is identical for $b=0$ and
$b=1$, so it cancels from $P_1-P_0$. Since the row indices within each
cycle are distinct, a fixed row occurs at most twice in the product of
the two cycle monomials and hence contributes at most four random
factors. The fourth-moment assumption therefore bounds every moment of
the $\xi$ variables which occurs here by a constant depending only on
$K$.

Only the following elementary Gaussian formulas are needed. If
$Z\sim N(0,P)$, then
\begin{align}
    \mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[Z_aZ_b\right]&=P_{ab},\label{eq:Gaussian second moment}\\
    \mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[Z_aZ_bZ_cZ_d\right]
      &=P_{ab}P_{cd}+P_{ac}P_{bd}+P_{ad}P_{bc},
        \label{eq:Gaussian fourth moment}
\end{align}
and a product of an odd number of coordinates has mean zero. In the
present case, independence across rows and
$P=I_n-UU^\top$ give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:projected Gaussian covariance}
    \mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[G^\perp_{j,i}G^\perp_{j',i'}\right]
    =\mathbbm{1}_{\{j=j'\}}\left(\mathbbm{1}_{\{i=i'\}}-u_i^\top u_{i'}\right).
\end{equation}
Thus \eqref{eq:Gaussian second moment}--\eqref{eq:Gaussian fourth moment},
followed by expanding each covariance in
\eqref{eq:projected Gaussian covariance}, writes every summand in
\eqref{eq:low rank variance expansion} as a sum of at most $C^k$ terms.
Each such term consists of bounded coefficients, factors involving the
vectors $u_i$, and explicit requirements that certain row indices and
column indices in the two cycles be equal.

We now bound one of these terms. Say that an edge of the first cycle is
matched to an edge of the second if the first term in
\eqref{eq:projected Gaussian covariance} is used for their two
$G^\perp$ factors. The indicator in that formula then requires both the
row and the column index of the two edges to be equal. Such a term
cannot match two $G^\perp$ factors within one cycle: their row indices
are either different, or they are the two edges incident to the same
row and their column indices are different. Hence all matched edges are
shared by the two cycles.

Unless all $2k$ edges are matched, the matched edges form disjoint
paths. Indeed, every vertex has degree two in either cycle, so a
connected set of shared edges is either a path or the entire cycle; the
latter is exactly the all-$G^\perp$ term already cancelled above. Let
$s$ be the number of these paths. A path of $r$ edges has $r+1$
vertices. Once the labels in the first cycle are chosen, the equality
requirements prescribe the corresponding $r+1$ alternating row and
column labels in the second cycle.

We now sum all terms having fixed locations and orientations for these
paths. Let $r$ be the number of matched edges, and let $a$ and $b$ be
the numbers of row vertices and column vertices, respectively, lying
in the paths. Since a path has one more vertex than edge,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:path vertices}
    a+b=r+s.
\end{equation}
The row labels have at most $m^{2k-a}$ possible values: without the
paths the two cycles have $2k$ row labels, while the value of each of
the $a$ rows in the second cycle is prescribed by the first.

It remains to sum the column labels. Every occurrence of a matrix entry
which is not part of a matched pair carries one factor $u_i$. After the
$b$ shared column vertices are merged, there are $2k-b$ column
positions. Exactly $r-b$ of them are internal column vertices of the
paths, incident only to matched edges, and hence carry no $u_i$ factor;
every other column position carries two. A position carrying no such
factor has at most $n$ possible labels. A position carrying two is
summed using
\begin{equation}\label{eq:orthonormal row sum}
    \sum_{i=1}^n u_i u_i^\top=I_d.
\end{equation}
The requirement that the columns within either cycle be distinct does
not enlarge this bound: after some labels have been fixed, the relevant
sum has the form
\[
    \sum_{i\notin S}u_i u_i^\top
    =I_d-\sum_{i\in S}u_i u_i^\top,
\]
whose operator norm is at most one. Since $d\le2$ and every row
contributes a moment of at most four bounded random variables, the
remaining finite-dimensional sums contribute at most $C^k$. The full
column sum is therefore at most $C^k n^{r-b}$.

Including the normalization in
\eqref{eq:low rank variance expansion}, the contribution of the fixed
paths is at most
\begin{align}
    \frac{C^k m^{2k-a}n^{r-b}}{(mn)^k}
    &=C^k\left(\frac mn\right)^{k-a}n^{r-a-b}
      \le C^k n^{-s},\label{eq:path contribution bound}
\end{align}
where we used \eqref{eq:path vertices} and the compact range of $m/n$.
This is the entire counting step: the exponent $s$ appears because each
path has one more vertex than edge.

There are at most $C^k$ choices made when expanding the matrix factors
and the Gaussian moments, and at most $k^{4s}$ choices for the endpoints
and orientations of $s$ paths. The total contribution from terms with
$s\ge1$ is consequently at most
\[
    C^k\sum_{s\ge1}
       \left(\frac{k^4}{n}\right)^s.
\]
If $s=0$, the two centered monomials in
\eqref{eq:low rank variance expansion} are independent unless their row
tuples share a value. For each of the $k^2$ possible positions of such
a shared value, choosing the first row tuple leaves at most $m^{k-1}$
choices for the second. The same column summation as above bounds these
terms by
\[
    \frac{C^k k^2m^{2k-1}}{(mn)^k}
    =\frac{C^k k^2}{m}\left(\frac mn\right)^k.
\]
Since $m/n$ remains in a compact subset of $(0,\infty)$ and
$k=O(\log n)$, we obtain the stronger bound
\begin{equation}\label{eq:absolute low rank variance}
    \mathrm{Var}(Z_k)\le \frac{C^k k^C}{m}.
\end{equation}
Finally, a direct calculation gives
\[
    \mathrm{Var}(C_k(m,M^{(0)}))
    =2k\frac{(m)_k(n)_k}{m^kn^k}\ge1
\]
for all sufficiently large $n$. After increasing $C$,
\eqref{eq:absolute low rank variance} proves
\eqref{eq:low rank variance} for $k\ge2$.

For $k=1$, the same estimate follows directly from
\[
    C_1(m,M^{(1)})-C_1(m,M^{(0)})
    =(mn)^{-1/2}\sum_{j=1}^m
      \left(\|\xi_j^{(1)}\|_2^2-\|\xi_j^{(0)}\|_2^2\right). \qedhere
\]

title: Proof
body_md:
The variance identity \eqref{eq:null cycle variance} is immediate for
$k=1$. For $k\ge2$, two Gaussian cycle monomials have nonzero covariance
only when they represent the same unoriented cycle, which has $2k$
choices of starting point and orientation. This gives the first equality
in \eqref{eq:null cycle variance}; the second follows from
$(s)_k/s^k=1+O(k^2/s)$.

For a single planted solution, the scalar $\xi_j^{(x)}$ is centered by
symmetry and has fourth moment bounded by $(\kappa/r)^4$ and hence by $\kappa^4$. Thus \cref{lem:low-rank-cycle-resampling} applies with
$d=1$, $U=\hat x$, and $\Sigma=\psi_{\kappa/r}^2$. Since
\[
    \mu(\hat x)=\|\hat x\|_\infty^2
    \le \frac{\log^2 n}{nr^2},
    \qquad
    D=\sqrt\alpha(\psi_{\kappa/r}^2-1)
      =2B_{\kappa/r,\alpha},
\]
\eqref{eq:B contraction} and \eqref{eq:low rank mean} together give
\eqref{eq:cycles-x-mean}. Moreover, uniformly for $k\le T$,
\[
    C^k k^C\bigl(\mu(\hat x)+m^{-1}\bigr)
    \le n^{-1+\lambda\log C+o(1)}.
\]
After decreasing $\lambda$ so that $\lambda\log C<1/4$, then
\eqref{eq:low rank variance} gives \eqref{eq:cycles-x-var}.

For a planted pair, let
\[
    \Sigma_\theta
    :=\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\xi_j^{(x,y)}(\xi_j^{(x,y)})^\top\right],
    \qquad
    D_\theta:=\sqrt\alpha(\Sigma_\theta-I_2).
\]
The full row covariance is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pair planted covariance}
    \mathrm{Cov}(G_j^{(x,y)}+\tau_j^{(x,y)})
    =I_n+U(\Sigma_\theta-I_2)U^\top.
\end{equation}
This identity includes the mixed $\hat x\hat z^\top$ terms. At
$\theta=0$, the two conditioning events are independent, and hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Sigma zero}
    \Sigma_0=\begin{pmatrix}
        \psi_{\kappa/r}^2&0\\
        0&\psi_{\kappa/\hat r}^2
    \end{pmatrix},
    \qquad
    D_0=\begin{pmatrix}
        2B_{\kappa/r,\alpha}&0\\
        0&2B_{\kappa/\hat r,\alpha}
    \end{pmatrix}.
\end{equation}
The map $\theta\mapsto\Sigma_\theta$ is analytic near zero, uniformly
for $r,\hat r\in I$. Let $J=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$. The change of
variables $W_2\mapsto-W_2$ in \eqref{eq:pair conditioning event} gives
\[
    \Sigma_{-\theta}=J\Sigma_\theta J,
    \qquad D_{-\theta}=JD_\theta J.
\]
Hence $\mathrm{tr}(D_\theta^k)$ is even in $\theta$. By
\eqref{eq:B contraction}, $\|D_\theta\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ is uniformly
bounded above by a constant smaller than one for the present range of
$\theta$. Taylor's theorem therefore gives, uniformly for $k\le T$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pair trace expansion}
    \mathrm{tr}(D_\theta^k)
    =(2B_{\kappa/r,\alpha})^k
     +(2B_{\kappa/\hat r,\alpha})^k+O(k^2\theta^2).
\end{equation}

Finally, \eqref{eq:y in xz basis} and the definition of the typical set
give
\[
    \mu(U)=\max_i(\hat x_i^2+\hat z_i^2)
    \le C\frac{\log^2 n}{n}.
\]
The conditional vector in \eqref{eq:pair conditioning event} has
uniformly bounded fourth moments. Applying
\cref{lem:low-rank-cycle-resampling}, then using
$|\theta|\le n^{-1/2}\log n$ and \eqref{eq:pair trace expansion}, proves
\eqref{eq:cycles-xy-mean}. After decreasing $\lambda$ once more, the
variance estimate \eqref{eq:low rank variance} proves
\eqref{eq:cycles-xy-var}.

name: Endpoint profile estimate

label: eq:p2'-bound
title: Proof
body_md:
As $F_2$ is even in $\theta$, it suffices to take
$\theta=-1+\epsilon$, so that $\theta \in (-1,0)$. Let $a=\kappa/r$ and $b=\kappa/\hat r$. Note that $p^{(2)}(a,b,\theta)$ is bounded away from zero for all $\theta$. Hence, applying the
derivative formula \eqref{eq:energy_derivative}, it holds uniformly for
$t\in[\epsilon/2,\epsilon]$,
\begin{align*}
    \partial_\theta\log p^{(2)}(a,b,-1+t) 
    \le-c \,t^{-1/2} \,\exp\left\{-\frac{(a-b)^2}{4t}\right\}\,.
\end{align*}
Recalling the assumption on $(r-\hat r)^2$, the exponent above is at most of order $-c_0\log(1/\epsilon)$. Hence, taking $c_0$ sufficiently small,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:p2'-bound}
    \partial_\theta\log p^{(2)}(a,b,-1+t) \le -t^{-.49}.
\end{equation}
Since
$p^{(2)}(a,b,-1+\epsilon/2)\le\min\{p(a),p(b)\}$,
integrating \eqref{eq:p2'-bound} from $\epsilon/2$ to $\epsilon$
gives:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:uniform endpoint probability estimate}
   \log p^{(2)}(a,b,-1+\epsilon) \le \log\min\left\{p(a),\,p(b)\right\} -c\,\epsilon^{.51}.
\end{equation}

It remains to control the entropy. Let $(X,Y)$ have law
$\mu_{r,\hat r,-1+\epsilon}^{(2)}$, and set
\[
    \delta:=\mathbb{P}_{}\left[X+Y\ne0\right],
    \qquad
    v:=\mathrm{Var}(X+Y)=(r-\hat r)^2+2r\hat r\epsilon.
\]
Since $X+Y$ is integer-valued, $\delta\le v$. Moreover, by the fact that the Gaussian maximizes entropy among real-valued random variables with fixed variance, it holds for any random variable $Z$,
\[
    H(Z)\le\frac12\log\left(2\pi e\,\mathrm{Var}(Z)\right)\,.
\]
This will be used in conjunction the crude upper bound $\mathrm{Var}(X+Y\mid X+Y = 0) \le v/\delta$.
In total, by the chain rule for entropy,
\begin{align*}
    H(X,Y)
    &\le H(X)+H(\mathbbm{1}_{\{X+Y\ne0\}})
       +\delta\, H(X+Y\mid X+Y\ne0)\\
    &\le H(X)+H(\mathbbm{1}_{\{X+Y\ne0\}})
       +\frac\delta2\log\left(2\pi e
          \,\frac v\delta\right).
\end{align*}
Since
$H(X)\le H(\mu_r)$ and $\delta\le v$, the last display is at most
\[
    H(\mu_r)+Cv\log(1/v).
\]
Interchanging $X$ and $Y$ gives the same estimate with
$H(\mu_{\hat r})$ in place of $H(\mu_r)$. Our assumption implies
$v=O(\epsilon\log(1/\epsilon))$, and hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:uniform endpoint entropy estimate}
    H(\mu_{r,\hat r,-1+\epsilon}^{(2)})
    \le\min\{H(\mu_r),H(\mu_{\hat r})\}
       +O(\epsilon\log^2(1/\epsilon)).
\end{equation}
The error in \eqref{eq:uniform endpoint entropy estimate} is
$o(\epsilon^{.51})$. Moreover,
\[
    \min\{H(\mu_r),H(\mu_{\hat r})\}
    +\alpha\log\min\{p(a),p(b)\}
    \le\min\{F_1(\kappa,\alpha,r),F_1(\kappa,\alpha,\hat r)\}.
\]
Combining the last two displays with
\eqref{eq:uniform endpoint probability estimate} proves the lemma.

label: eq:Y-single-Gaussian
title: Proof
body_md:
Under the conditional law given $\{x\in\mathbf{X}\}$,
\eqref{eq:Y rho representation} gives the identity
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Y-single-Gaussian}
     Y_T(m,G,\kappa/r)
    =\langle\rho_r,V(G)-\rho_r\rangle+\frac12s_r.
\end{equation}
Similarly, under the conditional law given $\{x,y\in\mathbf{X}\}$, we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Y-pair-Gaussian}
\begin{aligned}
    Y_T(m,G,\kappa/r)
    &=\langle\rho_r,V(G)-\rho_r-\rho_{\hat r}\rangle
      +\frac12s_r+\langle\rho_r,\rho_{\hat r}\rangle,\\
    Y_T(m,G,\kappa/\hat r)
    &=\langle\rho_{\hat r},V(G)-\rho_r-\rho_{\hat r}\rangle
      +\frac12s_{\hat r}+\langle\rho_r,\rho_{\hat r}\rangle.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Letting $W_T\sim N(0,I_T)$, the classical formula for the moment-generating function of a Gaussian gives
\[
    \mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\exp\left\{-\langle\rho_r,W_T\rangle-\frac12s_r\right\}\right]=1,
    \qquad
    \mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\exp\left\{-2\langle\rho_r,W_T\rangle-s_r\right\}\right]
    =e^{s_r}=O(1).
\]
This will be used shortly in conjunction with \eqref{eq:Y-single-Gaussian} and the normal approximation \eqref{eq:joint normal x}, which asserts $V(G) - \rho_r\approx W_T$ in distribution.
We also have
\[
    \mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\exp\left\{
        -\langle\rho_r+\rho_{\hat r},W_T\rangle
        -\frac{s_r+s_{\hat r}}2
        -2\langle\rho_r,\rho_{\hat r}\rangle
    \right\}\right]
    =e^{-\langle\rho_r,\rho_{\hat r}\rangle}.
\]
Similarly, this will be used shortly in conjunction with \eqref{eq:Y-pair-Gaussian} and \eqref{eq:joint normal xy}, which asserts $V(G) - \rho_r - \rho_{\hat{r}} \approx W_T$.


We next reintroduce into our approximation the cutoff $\mathbbm{1}( \cdot \ge -L)$ from the definition of $\mathcal{W}_r$. Recall that $L := \sqrt{\log n}$; moreover, as noted above, $s_r$ and hence $\|\rho_r\|_2$ are uniformly bounded for all $r \in I$. Letting $g: x\mapsto  \exp(-x) \mathbbm{1}(x \ge -L)$, these estimates and the formula for the Gaussian density imply that, for some constant $c := c_{\kappa} > 0$,
\begin{align*}
    \mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[g\big(\langle\rho_r,W_T\rangle+\tfrac12s_r\big)\right]
    &=1+O(n^{-c}),\\
    \mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[g\big(\langle\rho_r,W_T\rangle+\tfrac12s_r\big)^2\right]
    &=O(1),\\
    \mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[
    g\big(\langle\rho_r,W_T\rangle+\tfrac12s_r
    +\langle\rho_r,\rho_{\hat r}\rangle\big)
    g\big(\langle\rho_{\hat r},W_T\rangle+\tfrac12s_{\hat r}
    +\langle\rho_r,\rho_{\hat r}\rangle\big)\right]
    &=e^{-\langle\rho_r,\rho_{\hat r}\rangle}+O(n^{-c}).
\end{align*}


It remains to transfer these Gaussian calculations to the actual cycle counts. We first need a smooth approximation for $g$. Fix a nondecreasing
$\chi\in\mathcal C^\infty(\mathbb{R};[0,1])$ that is zero on $(-\infty,0]$ and one on $[1,\infty)$. Set
\[
    \chi_-(x):=\chi(x+L),\qquad
    \chi_+(x):=\chi(x+L+1),\qquad
    g_\pm(x):=e^{-x}\chi_\pm(x).
\]
Then
\[
    \chi_-(x)\le\mathbbm{1}(x\ge-L)\le\chi_+(x),
    \qquad g_-(x)\le g(x)\le g_+(x).
\]
Replacing $g$ by $g_\pm$ changes the Gaussian expectations above by $O(n^{-c})$, after decreasing $c$ if necessary, since these functions differ only on $[-L-1,-L+1]$.
We then apply \eqref{eq:joint normal x} to
\[
    u\longmapsto
    g_\pm\left(
        \langle\rho_r,u\rangle + \frac12s_r\right), \qquad \text{ and } u\longmapsto
    g_\pm\left(
        \langle\rho_r,u\rangle  + \frac12s_r\right)^2\,.
\]
Similarly, we apply
\eqref{eq:joint normal xy} to
\[
\begin{aligned}
    u\longmapsto\;&
    g_\pm\left(
        \langle\rho_r,u\rangle+\frac12s_r
        +\langle\rho_r,\rho_{\hat r}\rangle
    \right) \times
    g_\pm\left(
        \langle\rho_{\hat r},u\rangle+\frac12s_{\hat r}
        +\langle\rho_r,\rho_{\hat r}\rangle
    \right).
\end{aligned}
\]
We claim that the first three derivatives of all three of the above maps are bounded by $O(e^{2L})$. Indeed, the functions $\chi_\pm(\cdot)$ have uniformly bounded derivatives by construction, and the cutoffs $\chi_\pm(\cdot)$ in the definition of $g_\pm$ enforce the uniform bounds $0 \le g_\pm(\cdot) \le e^{L+1}$. Hence, the error incurred by the above invocations of the Gaussian
approximations \eqref{eq:joint normal x} and \eqref{eq:joint normal xy} is at most
\[
    O(n^{-1/5}e^{2L})
    =O\left(
        \exp\left\{-\frac15\log n+2\sqrt{\log n}\right\}
      \right)
    =o(1).
\]

title: Remark
body_md: The definition $L:=\sqrt{\log n}$ was somewhat arbitrary and taken for concreteness. Nonetheless, the above argument enforces that $L$ should satisfy $\omega(1) \le L \le o(\log n)$, as two tensions must be (loosely) balanced. First, we need $L$ small enough that $e^{2L}=n^{o(1)}$, so that the cutoff $\chi_\pm$ is sufficiently smooth for approximation; at the same time, $L$ should be large enough that $e^{-cL^2}=o(1)$, so that the cutoff $\chi$ does not affect the limiting Gaussian expectation.

$\alpha_c:=\alpha_c(\kappa)$,  let

       \left(\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[W^2\mid |W|\le\kappa/r_c\right]-1\right), \quad 
    \gamma_c:=-\left.
       \frac{\partial^2}{\partial v^2}
       F_1(\kappa,\alpha_c,\sqrt v)
       \right|_{v=r_c^2}, \quad 
    C_\kappa:=
       \left(\gamma_c\mathrm{Var}_{X\sim\mu_{r_c}}(X^2)\right)^{-1/2}.

\begin{equation}\label{eq:critical window distribution}
    f_\kappa(t):=\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\exp\left\{-\frac{C_\kappa}{2}
                    p_c^t e^{W_c}\right\}\right], \qquad  W_c\sim\mathcal N\left(
       \frac14\log(1-4B_c^2),
       -\frac12\log(1-4B_c^2)
       \right).
\end{equation}
Then, for each fixed $T>0$, uniformly over $t\in[-T,T]$ such that

    \mathbb{P}_{}\left[ \mathbf{X}_{n,m,\kappa} = \emptyset \right] = f_\kappa(t)+o(1).
\end{equation}

$\lim_{t\to-\infty}f_\kappa(t)=0$ and
$\lim_{t\to+\infty}f_\kappa(t)=1$.

body_md:
Fix $C<\infty$ and suppose that $|s|\le C\log n$. Recalling
$w_n:=\log\log n$, we first claim that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:critical radius truncation}
    \sum_{\substack{r\in\mathcal R_n:\
                    \sqrt n\,|r-r_c|>w_n}}
       \mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\mathcal{Z}_r\right]
    =o(p_c^s).
\end{equation}

Indeed, \eqref{eq:F1-capacity-sign} gives
\[
    F_1(\kappa,\alpha_c,r_c)=0.
\]
The radius-truncation argument in the proof of
\cref{thm:truncated 1mm}, with
$(\alpha,r_*)=(\alpha_c,r_c)$, applies mutatis mutandis. Hence, for $r$ near $r_c$,
\[
    N(r)p(\kappa/r)^{\alpha_c n}
    \le K n^{-1/2}e^{-cn(r-r_c)^2}.
\]
The only additional factor is $p(\kappa/r)^s$. A first-order expansion
gives
$
    p(\kappa/r)^s
    =p_c^s\exp\{O(|s||r-r_c|)\}.
$
Then,
\begin{align*}
    \mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\mathcal{Z}_r\right]
    &\le K n^{-1/2}p_c^s
       \exp\{-cn(r-r_c)^2+K|s||r-r_c|\}\\
    &\le K' n^{-1/2}p_c^s
       \exp\{-c'n(r-r_c)^2\},
\end{align*}
where the second inequality follows by completing the square and using
$s^2/n=o(1)$. Thus the proof of \eqref{eq:F1 trunc mid} applies without
further change.

On any fixed compact set away from $r_c$, it holds uniformly that
$p(\kappa/r)^s/p_c^s= n^{O(1)}$, while $\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\mathcal{Z}_r\right]$ is already exponentially smaller than $\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\mathcal{Z}_I\right]$. Finally, for large $r$, we have $p(\kappa/r)^s\le (Kr)^{C\log n}$ for some $K<\infty$. Since $\alpha_c>1$, the
summation in \eqref{eq:F1 trunc extreme} still decays exponentially. Hence, arguing as in \cref{thm:truncated 1mm} yields
\eqref{eq:critical radius truncation}.

It therefore suffices to sum over radii satisfying
$\sqrt n\,|r-r_c|\le w_n$. Uniformly over these radii,
\cref{prop:1d-lattice-count} gives
\[
    \mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\mathcal{Z}_r\right]
    =\frac{1+o(1)}
      {\sqrt{2\pi n\mathrm{Var}_{X\sim\mu_r}(X^2)}}
      \exp\{nF_1(\kappa,\alpha_c,r)\}
      p(\kappa/r)^s.
\]
Recalling that $F_1(\kappa,\alpha_c,r_c)=0$ and that $r_c$ is the
maximizer of $F_1$, the definition of $\gamma_c$ gives
\[
    F_1(\kappa,\alpha_c,r)
    =-\frac{\gamma_c}{2}(r^2-r_c^2)^2
      +O(|r^2-r_c^2|^3)
    =-\frac{\gamma_c}{2}(r^2-r_c^2)^2+o(n^{-1}).
\]
Moreover, first-order expansions give
\[
    p(\kappa/r)^s
    =p_c^s\exp\{O(|s||r-r_c|)\}
    =(1+o(1))p_c^s, \quad
    \mathrm{Var}_{X\sim\mu_r}(X^2)
    =(1+o(1))\mathrm{Var}_{X\sim\mu_{r_c}}(X^2).
\]
Consequently, 
\begin{align*} \mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\mathcal{Z}\right] &=(1+o(1)) \frac{p_c^s} {\sqrt{2\pi n\mathrm{Var}_{X\sim\mu_{r_c}}(X^2)}} \sum_{\substack{r\in\mathcal{R}_n\\ \sqrt n\,|r-r_c|\le\log\log n}} \exp\left\{-\frac{\gamma_c n}{2}(r^2-r_c^2)^2\right\} +o(p_c^s). \\ &= (1+o(1)) \frac{p_c^s} {\sqrt{\gamma_c\mathrm{Var}_{X\sim\mu_{r_c}}(X^2)}} =(C_\kappa+o(1))p_c^s. \end{align*}
Between the first and second lines, we have used that the Gaussian sum converges to $\sqrt{2\pi n/\gamma_c}$.

body_md:
We prove the claims in \cref{thmStructure} in reverse order, beginning with item \ref{item:lognormal}. We begin by giving the more precise statement of the log-normal limit.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:lognormal}
Let $\kappa, \alpha, n, m$ be as in \cref{thmStructure}. Let
\[
    B_*:=\frac{\sqrt\alpha}{2}
       \left(\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[W^2\mid |W|\le\kappa/r_*\right]-1\right)
\]
and
\[
    W_{\kappa,\alpha}\sim\mathcal N\left(
       \frac14\log(1-4B_*^2),
       -\frac12\log(1-4B_*^2)
       \right),
\]
then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:main lognormal limit}
    \sup_{s\in\mathbb{R}}
    \left|
\mathbb{P}_{}\left[\mathcal{Z}>e^s\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\mathcal{Z}\right]\right]-\mathbb{P}_{}\left[W_{\kappa,\alpha}>s\right]
    \right|=o(1).
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof} 
Let $\alpha_n=m/n$. Note that \cref{hyp:maxima} is robust to sufficiently small perturbations in $\alpha$: item~(2) and the local expansion at
$\theta=0$ control small overlaps, \cref{lemma:F2-endpoint-uniform}
controls a neighborhood of $\theta=\pm1$, and continuity and compactness
control the remaining values of $\theta$.
Consequently, \cref{hyp:maxima} holds throughout some compact interval
$J\subset(1,\alpha_c(\kappa)]$ containing $\alpha$ in its interior.
For all sufficiently large $n$, we have $\alpha_n\in J$ and
$m\le\alpha_c(\kappa)n-\eta\log n$ for some fixed $\eta>0$, so the results of
\cref{sec:second moment method} apply. Let
$I=I_n(\kappa,\alpha_n)$ and write $\mathcal{Z}^{\text{\tiny{typ}}}=\mathcal{Z}_I^{\text{\tiny{typ}}}$. By
\cref{thm:truncated 1mm,lemma:conditional 2mm},
\begin{equation}\label{eq:full versus typical}
    \frac{\mathcal{Z}-\mathcal{Z}^{\text{\tiny{typ}}}}{\mathcal{Z}^{\text{\tiny{typ}}}}=o_{\mathbb P}(1),
    \qquad
    \frac{\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\mathcal{Z}\right]}{\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\mathcal{Z}^{\text{\tiny{typ}}}\right]}=1+o(1).
\end{equation}
Indeed, the numerator in the first ratio is at most
$e^{-c(\log\log n)^2}\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\mathcal{Z}^{\text{\tiny{typ}}}\right]$ with high probability, while the denominator is lower bounded via
\eqref{eq:conditional 2mm - tail goal}. Hence, with high probability,
\begin{align*}
    \log\frac{\mathcal{Z}}{\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\mathcal{Z}\right]}
    &=
    \log\frac{\mathcal{Z}^{\text{\tiny{typ}}}}{\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\mathcal{Z}^{\text{\tiny{typ}}}\right]}
    +\log\frac{\mathcal{Z}}{\mathcal{Z}^{\text{\tiny{typ}}}}
    +\log\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\mathcal{Z}^{\text{\tiny{typ}}}\right]}{\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\mathcal{Z}\right]} \stackrel{\eqref{eq:full versus typical}}=
    \log\frac{\mathcal{Z}^{\text{\tiny{typ}}}}{\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\mathcal{Z}^{\text{\tiny{typ}}}\right]}
    +o_{\mathbb P}(1),
\end{align*}
Since $\alpha_n\to\alpha$, continuity
gives $r_*(\kappa,\alpha_n)\to r_*$ and $B_{\kappa/r_*(\kappa,\alpha_n),\alpha_n}\to B_*$.
Thus, the mean and variance of the Gaussian $W_{\alpha_n}$ in
\eqref{eq:conditional 2mm - scaling limit goal} converge to those of
$W_{\kappa,\alpha}$. Since these Gaussian densities are uniformly
bounded, the $o_{\mathbb P}(1)$ perturbation above does not affect the
Kolmogorov distance. This establishes \eqref{eq:main lognormal limit}, and also item \ref{item:lognormal} of \cref{thmStructure}. \end{proof}

We next prove item \ref{item:typical empirical} of \cref{thmStructure}, the assertion about empirical distributions. For fixed
$r\in I$, consider an empirical distribution $\nu$ of a vector in
$\Lambda_n^{\text{\tiny{typ}}}(r)$. 
Writing $\mu_r(k)=e^{a_rk^2+b_r}$, we have
\[
    \sum_k k^2\nu(k)=r^2=\sum_k k^2\mu_r(k).
\]
Hence,
\begin{align*}
    D(\nu\|\mu_r)
    =-H(\nu)-\sum_k\nu(k)(a_rk^2+b_r)&=-H(\nu)-a_rr^2-b_r =H(\mu_r)-H(\nu).
\end{align*}
On the other hand, there are at most $(n+1)^{2\log n}$ possible empirical
distributions $\nu$ since typical vectors $x$ satisfy $\|x\|_\infty\le \log n$ by construction. Moreover, standard counting considerations give that each empirical distribution $\nu$ corresponds to at most $e^{nH(\nu)}$
vectors. Hence, for every $s>0$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:empirical type bound}
    \left|\left\{x\in\Lambda_n^{\text{\tiny{typ}}}(r):
       D(\nu_x\|\mu_r)\ge s\right\}\right|
    \le \exp\{nH(\mu_r)-ns+O((\log n)^2)\}.
\end{equation}
We remark that this is the main computation in the proof of
Sanov's theorem; however, it is more convenient here to use the explicit bound above rather than quote the full theorem.

Let $\epsilon_n=n^{-1/2}(\log n)^{3}$ and define the set of solutions with ``atypical'' empirical distribution by
\[
    A_0:=\left\{x\in\mathbf{X}_{n,m,\kappa}^{\text{\tiny{typ}}}:
       \|\nu_x-\mu_{r_x}\|_{\mathrm{TV}}>\epsilon_n\right\},
    \qquad r_x:=\|x\|_2/\sqrt n.
\]
Combining this with \eqref{eq:empirical type bound} gives
\begin{align*}
    \mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[|A_0|\right]
    &\le
    e^{-2n\epsilon_n^2+O((\log n)^2)}
    \sum_{r\in I}e^{nH(\mu_r)}p(\kappa/r)^m.
\end{align*}
Applying the local central limit
theorem to \cref{prop:1d-lattice-count}, and then using \eqref{eq:E[Z] - typical} to restrict to typical vectors, it holds uniformly over $r\in I$, 
\[
    e^{nH(\mu_r)}
    \le C\sqrt n\,|\Lambda_n^{\text{\tiny{typ}}}(r)|.
\]
Hence, as $n\epsilon_n^2 = \omega((\log n)^2)$,
\[
    \mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[|A_0|\right]
    \le e^{-cn\epsilon_n^2}\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\mathcal{Z}^{\text{\tiny{typ}}}\right].
\]
Consequently, Markov's inequality and
\eqref{eq:conditional 2mm - tail goal} give
\begin{align*}
    \mathbb{P}_{}\left[\frac{|A_0|}{\mathcal{Z}^{\text{\tiny{typ}}}}>
             e^{-cn\epsilon_n^2/2}\right]
    &\le
    \mathbb{P}_{}\left[\mathcal{Z}^{\text{\tiny{typ}}}<(\log n)^{-1/2}\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\mathcal{Z}^{\text{\tiny{typ}}}\right]\right]
      +(\log n)^{1/2}e^{-cn\epsilon_n^2/2}=o(1).
\end{align*}
That is, with high probability, the proportion of solutions with atypical empirical distribution is vanishing:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:empirical good solutions}
    \frac{|A_0|}{\mathcal{Z}^{\text{\tiny{typ}}}}=o_{\mathbb P}(1).
\end{equation}
Of course, our definition of $A_0$ compares to $\mu_{r_x}$ rather than $\mu_{r_*}$; it remains to correct for this. 
Since $\alpha_n\to\alpha$ and $I$ is centered at
$r_*(\kappa,\alpha_n)$,
\[
    \sup_{r\in I}|r-r_*|
    \le\frac{w_n}{\sqrt n}
       +|r_*(\kappa,\alpha_n)-r_*|
    =o(1).
\]
Continuity of the discrete Gaussian in its variance therefore gives
\[
    \sup_{r\in I}\|\mu_r-\mu_{r_*}\|_{\mathrm{TV}}=o(1).
\]
Thus every $x\in\mathbf{X}_{n,m,\kappa}^{\text{\tiny{typ}}}\setminus A_0$ satisfies
\[
    \|\nu_x-\mu_{r_*}\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
    \le\epsilon_n+
       \sup_{r\in I}\|\mu_r-\mu_{r_*}\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
    =o(1).
\]
Combining the above estimates readily yields
item \ref{item:typical empirical} of \cref{thmStructure}; moreover, we remark that tracking the errors more carefully above leads to the quantitative rate $\|\nu_x - \mu_{r_*}\|_{\mathrm{TV}} \le n^{-1/2}(\log n)^{c}$. \\

We establish item \ref{item:typical orthogonal} next, which asserts the near-orthogonality of typical solutions. Let $P^{\text{\tiny{typ}}}$ be the number of ordered pairs $(x,y)$ of typical
solutions $x,y\in\mathbf{X}_{n,m,\kappa}^{\text{\tiny{typ}}}$ such that
$y\notin\{x,-x\}$ and
$|\langle x,y\rangle|>\sqrt n\log n$. The unweighted estimates in the proof of
\cref{lemma:conditional 2mm}, obtained by removing the weights in the
arguments for
\eqref{eq:2mm-near intermediate}, \eqref{eq:2mm-bulk}, and
\eqref{eq:2mm-extreme off diagonal}, give
\[
    \mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[P^{\text{\tiny{typ}}}\right]=o\bigl(\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\mathcal{Z}^{\text{\tiny{typ}}}\right]^2\bigr).
\]
It follows from \eqref{eq:conditional 2mm - scaling limit goal} and
Markov's inequality that $P^{\text{\tiny{typ}}}/(\mathcal{Z}^{\text{\tiny{typ}}})^2=o_{\mathbb P}(1)$.
Except for pairs $(x,y)$ with $y\in\{x, -x\}$ (which are negligible in number compared to $\mathcal{Z}^2$), all remaining ordered pairs have at least one endpoint outside the
typical set and hence number at most
$2\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{Z}-\mathcal{Z}^{\text{\tiny{typ}}})$. Applying \eqref{eq:full versus typical}
yields item~(2).\\

It remains to prove item \ref{item:freezing}, namely freezing in Hamming distance. Let $\delta$ be the constant in \eqref{eq:strong freezing conclusion}; we will prove item \ref{item:freezing} with a modified constant $\delta'$. Since $I$
remains in a compact subset of $(1,\infty)$, there are $c,C>0$ such
that the sub-Gaussian estimate $\mu_r(k)\le Ce^{-ck^2}$ holds uniformly for $r\in I$. Thus, there exists
some fixed $M<\infty$ with
\[
    \sup_{r\in I}
    \mathbb{E}_{\mu_r\unskip\space}\left[X^2\mathbbm{1}_{\{|X|>M\}}\right]\le\frac{\delta^2}{32}.
\]
For all $n$ sufficiently large, we then have for every $x\in\mathbf{X}_{n,m,\kappa}^{\text{\tiny{typ}}}\setminus A_0$,
\begin{align*}
    \frac1n\sum_{i:\,|x_i|>M}x_i^2 &\le \mathbb{E}_{\mu_{r_x}\unskip\space}\left[X^2\mathbbm{1}_{\{|X|>M\}}\right]
      + 2(\log n)^2\epsilon_n \le\frac{\delta^2}{16}\,.
\end{align*}
That is, ``large'' coordinates do not contribute significantly to $\|x\|$. Next, choose $\delta'\in(0,1/2)$ so that
$2M^2\delta'\le\delta^2/16$. If
$x,x'\in\mathbf{X}_{n,m,\kappa}^{\text{\tiny{typ}}}\setminus A_0$ differ in at most
$2\delta' n$ coordinates, decomposing the set $\{i\,:\, x_i \neq x_i'\}$ based on whether $|x_i| > M$ or $|x_i| \le M$ (and similarly for $x_i'$) gives
\begin{align*}
    \|x-x'\|_2^2
    &\le2\sum_{i:x_i\ne x_i'}x_i^2
       +2\sum_{i:x_i\ne x_i'}(x_i')^2 \le4\left(\frac{\delta^2n}{16}+2M^2\delta'n\right)
    \le\frac{\delta^2n}{2}.
\end{align*}
This gives freezing with respect to Hamming distance for pairs of typical solution vectors. It remains to briefly handle freezing in the case that at least one of the solution vectors is atypical. Define
\[
    A:=(\mathbf{X}_{n,m,\kappa}\setminus\mathbf{X}_{n,m,\kappa}^{\text{\tiny{typ}}})\cup A_0,
\]
the set of solutions which are atypical in radius, infinity norm, or empirical distribution. Also define the set of typical solutions violating freezing as
\[
    B := \{x \in \mathbf{X}_{n,m,\kappa}\setminus A\,:\, \exists\,y\in (\mathbf{X}_{n,m,\kappa}\setminus A)\setminus\{x\},~\|x-y\|_2 \le \delta \sqrt{n}\}\,.
\]
By
\eqref{eq:full versus typical} and
\eqref{eq:empirical good solutions}, $|A|$ is negligible; by
\eqref{eq:strong freezing conclusion}, $|B|$ is also negligible. That is,
\[
    \frac{|A|}{\mathcal{Z}}=o_{\mathbb P}(1),
    \qquad
    \frac{|B|}{\mathcal{Z}}=o_{\mathbb P}(1).
\]

A fixed vector $y\in A$ can be within Hamming distance $\delta'n$ of at most one solution outside $A\cup B$.
Indeed, if two distinct solutions $x,x'\notin A\cup B$ were each within Hamming distance $\delta'n$ of $y$, then $x$ and $x'$ would differ in at most $2\delta'n$
coordinates. The preceding bound would give
$\|x-x'\|_2\le\delta\sqrt n$, so the definition of $B$ would imply $x,x'\in B$, which is a contradiction.

Therefore, the total
number of solutions $x \in \mathbf{X}_{n,m,\kappa}$ having at least one (different) solution within Hamming distance
$\delta' n$ is at most
\[
    2|A|+|B|=o_{\mathbb P}(\mathcal{Z}).
\]
This proves item \ref{item:freezing} and completes all parts of the proof of \cref{thmStructure}.

body_md:
We directly adapt the stopping-time argument of Sah and Sawhney
\cite[Section~2]{ss}, mutatis mutandis. There are some minor running differences due to the present model allowing for slight variation in the norms of the solutions. These are handled using the same type of Lipschitz estimates that have been used throughout the rest of the manuscript. We present the proof for completeness.

By assumption, \cref{hyp:maxima} holds at $\alpha_c$. The same stability argument used in the previous proof gives that \cref{hyp:maxima} also holds
throughout some interval $J=[\alpha_0,\alpha_c]$. We use
\cref{lemma:conditional 2mm} on this interval. Choose a sufficiently small fixed $\eta>0$ and reveal the first
\[
    m_0:=\lfloor\alpha_c n-\eta\log n\rfloor
\]
rows. Define $\mathcal F_{m_0}:=\sigma(G_1,\ldots,G_{m_0})$, and let $s_0 :=m_0-\alpha_c n$,
$I_0 :=I_n(\kappa,m_0/n)$, and
\[
    \mathcal T_0:=\bigcup_{r\in I_0}\Lambda_n^{\text{\tiny{typ}}}(r),
    \qquad
    \mathcal{Z}_0:=|\mathbf{X}_{n,m_0,\kappa}\cap\mathcal T_0|.
\]
Note that $\mathcal{T}_0$, which should be thought of as the surviving typical solutions at the precritical time, is $\mathcal{F}_{m_0}$--measurable. By \cref{lem:critical first moment,thm:truncated 1mm},
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pretime first moment}
    \mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\mathcal{Z}_0\right]=(C_\kappa+o(1))\,p_c^{s_0}.
\end{equation}
Choose $\eta$ small enough that
$\eta\log(1/p_c)<1/8$. Then
\cref{lemma:conditional 2mm} implies that with high probability, 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pretime good event1}
    \frac{\mathcal{Z}_0}{\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\mathcal{Z}_0\right]}
       \in\bigl((\log n)^{-1/2},(\log n)^{1/2}\bigr),
    \qquad
    \mathcal{Z}_0\le n^{1/4},
\end{equation}
and also, simultaneously for all pairs $x,y\in\mathbf{X}_{n,m_0,\kappa}\cap\mathcal T_0$ with
$y\notin\{x,-x\}$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pretime good event2}
    |\langle x,y\rangle|\le\sqrt n\log n\,.
\end{equation}



Fix $T<\infty$, let $m=\alpha_c n+t\in\mathbb N$ with $|t|\le T$, and
let $\ell=m-m_0$. Conditioned on $\mathcal F_{m_0}$, choose one
representative from each antipodal pair in
$\mathbf{X}_{n,m_0,\kappa}\cap\mathcal T_0$, and call the resulting set $S$.
Thus $|S|=\mathcal{Z}_0/2$. For a new standard Gaussian row $G_j=\sqrt nA_j$,
the vector
\[
    \left(\langle G_j,x/\|x\|_2\rangle\right)_{x\in S}
\]
is centered Gaussian with covariance matrix $R$ given by
\[
    R_{x,y}=\frac{\langle x,y\rangle}{\|x\|_2\|y\|_2}.
\]
Within the intersection of the high-probability events in \eqref{eq:pretime good event1} and \eqref{eq:pretime good event2}, the covariance $R$ trivializes:
\[
    \|R-I\|_{\mathrm{F}}
    \le C|S|\frac{\log n}{\sqrt n}=o(1).
\]
Consequently, using the formula for the relative entropy of multidimensional Gaussians readily gives
\[
    D\left(
       N(0,R)^{\otimes\ell}\,\middle\|\,N(0,I)^{\otimes\ell}
    \right)
    \le C\ell\,\|R-I\|_{\mathrm F}^2=o(1).
\]
In particular, Pinsker's inequality gives that the joint law for the Gaussian processes corresponding to the inner products of $S$ with the next
$\ell=O(\log n)$ rows is vanishingly close in total variation from the idealized law in
which all these Gaussian variables are independent. This is
the decoupling step in
\cite[Section~2]{ss}.

For $x\in S$ with $\|x\|_2=r_x\sqrt n$, its survival probability under the addition of $\ell$ fresh constraints is
\[
    q_x:=p(\kappa/r_x)^\ell.
\]
Next, the dependence on $x$ is removed from $q$. We claim:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:critical maximizing radius comparison}
    r_*(\kappa,m_0/n)=r_c+O_{\kappa,\eta}((\log n)/n).
\end{equation}
Indeed, let $\Phi(v,\beta):=\partial_vF_1(\kappa,\beta,\sqrt v)$. Then
$\Phi(v_c,\alpha_c)=0$ and
$\partial_v\Phi(v_c,\alpha_c)=-\gamma_c<0$. The implicit function
theorem therefore gives a $C^1$ function
$v_*(\beta)=r_*(\kappa,\beta)^2$ near $\alpha_c$, and hence
\[
    |v_*(\beta)-v_c|\le C|\beta-\alpha_c|,
\]
where $C$ depends only on $\kappa$. Since $v_c>0$ and $\eta$ is fixed,
this yields the claim. Consequently, we obtain that uniformly over $x\in S$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:varying radii survival}
    q_x=p_c^\ell
       \left(1+O\left(\frac{(\log n)(\log\log n)}{\sqrt n}\right)\right).
\end{equation}
Within the high probability events in \eqref{eq:pretime good event1} and \eqref{eq:pretime good event2},
$\mathcal{Z}_0p_c^\ell=O(\sqrt{\log n})$ almost surely by
\eqref{eq:conditional 2mm - tail goal} and
\eqref{eq:pretime first moment}, while
$p_c^\ell=n^{-\eta\log(1/p_c)+o(1)}=o(1)$. Hence
\eqref{eq:varying radii survival} and the expansion
$\log(1-z)=-z+O(z^2)$ let us estimate the probability that no solutions from $\mathcal{T}_0$ survive after the $m^\text{th}$ constraint:

\begin{equation}\label{eq:conditional extinction}
    \mathbb{P}_{}\left[\mathcal T_0 \cap \mathbf{X}_{n,m,\kappa} = \emptyset
          \mid \mathcal F_{m_0}\right]
    = \exp\left\{-\frac12p_c^\ell\mathcal{Z}_0\right\}+o(1).
\end{equation}
The factor $1/2$ appears because solutions occur in antipodal pairs.

It remains only to remove the restriction to the set of typical solutions, $\mathcal T_0$. Apply
\eqref{eq:critical radius truncation} with
$w_n=\frac12\log\log n$. Together with \eqref{eq:critical maximizing radius comparison} and the infinity-norm truncation
argument leading to \eqref{eq:E[Z] - typical}, which is uniform when
$m/n$ ranges in a fixed neighborhood of $\alpha_c$, we have uniformly for $|t|\le T$,
\[
    \mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\left|\mathbf{X}_{n,m,\kappa}\setminus\mathcal T_0\right|\right]=o(1).
\]
Thus Markov's inequality and \eqref{eq:conditional extinction} yield
\begin{equation}\label{eq:extinction from pretime}
    \mathbb{P}_{}\left[\mathbf{X}_{n,m,\kappa}=\emptyset\right]
    =\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\exp\left\{-\frac12p_c^\ell\mathcal{Z}_0\right\}\right]+o(1).
\end{equation}
Finally, as $m_0/n\to\alpha_c$, \eqref{eq:conditional 2mm - scaling limit goal} gives
\[
    \log\frac{\mathcal{Z}_0}{\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\mathcal{Z}_0\right]}
    \ \xrightarrow{\ d\ }\ W_c,
\]
Moreover,
\eqref{eq:pretime first moment} with $t := s_0 + \ell$ gives
\[
    \frac12p_c^\ell\,\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\mathcal{Z}_0\right]
    =\left(\frac{C_\kappa}{2}+o(1)\right)p_c^t.
\]
Since $(t,z)\mapsto\exp\left(-C_\kappa p_c^t e^{z}/2\right)$ is bounded and uniformly continuous on $[-T, T]\times \mathbb R$, it follows uniformly for $|t|\leq T$ that 
\[\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2}p_c^{\ell}\mathcal{Z}_0\right\}\right]=\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\exp\left\{-\frac{C_\kappa}{2} p_c^t e^{W_c}\right\}\right]+o(1).\]
Then \eqref{eq:extinction from pretime} gives, uniformly
for $|t| \le T$ and $\alpha_cn+t\in\mathbb N$,
\[
    \mathbb{P}_{}\left[\mathbf{X}_{n,m,\kappa}=\emptyset\right]
    =\mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[\exp\left\{-\frac{C_\kappa}{2}p_c^te^{W_c}\right\}\right]+o(1)
    =f_\kappa(t)+o(1).
\]
Finally, $p_c\in(0,1)$ and $e^{W_c}>0$ almost surely, so the dominated convergence theorem gives the claimed limits for $f_\kappa(t)$ as $t \to \pm \infty$.

body_md:
Write $S=(\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\})^2$ and
\[
    R=r^2-1,\qquad T=\hat r^2-1,\qquad s=r\hat r\theta.
\]
For $q(x,y)=Ax^2+Bxy+Cy^2$, the sum
$\sum_{(x,y)\in S}e^{-q(x,y)}$ is finite exactly when
$A,C>0$ and $B^2<4AC$. Also, no nonzero linear combination of $x^2,xy,y^2$ is
constant on $S$.

The results of \cite[Proposition~3.2, Theorems~3.3--3.4,
and Appendix~B.1]{wainwright-jordan} therefore reduce the claim
to the following check: for every nonzero quadratic $q(x,y)=Ax^2+Bxy+Cy^2$
bounded below on $S$,
\[
    Ar^2+Bs+C\hat r^2>\inf_{(x,y)\in S}q(x,y).
\]
Such a quadratic necessarily has $A,C\ge0$ and
$|B|\le2\sqrt{AC}$; otherwise it tends to $-\infty$ along
integer multiples of a suitable vector.
Taking $x,y\in\{-1,1\}$ gives
\[
    \inf_{(x,y)\in S}q(x,y)\le A+C-|B|.
\]
By the hypothesis, choose $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ such that
$|s|-1\le(1-\varepsilon)\sqrt{RT}$. Then
\begin{align*}
    Ar^2+Bs+C\hat r^2-(A+C-|B|)
    &=AR+CT+Bs+|B|\\
    &\ge AR+CT-(1-\varepsilon)\sqrt{RT}\,|B|\\
    &\ge\varepsilon(AR+CT)>0,
\end{align*}
where we used $|B|\le2\sqrt{AC}$ and
$2\sqrt{RATC}\le AR+CT$. The cited result gives the claimed density and unique coefficients.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $(h_j)_{j\ge0}$ be the orthonormal Hermite polynomials in
$L^2(\gamma)$, and expand
\[
    \frac{\mathbbm{1}_{\{|x|\le K\}}}{p(K)}
       =1+\sum_{j\ge1}a_jh_j(x).
\]
Symmetry gives $a_j=0$ for odd $j$, and correlated standard
Gaussians satisfy
\[
    \mathbb{E}_{\unskip\space}\left[h_j(W)h_\ell(W_\theta)\right]
       =\mathbbm{1}_{\{j=\ell\}}\theta^j.
\]
Consequently,
\[
    \frac{p^{(2)}(K,K,\theta)}{p(K)^2}
       =1+\sum_{j\ge1}a_{2j}^2\theta^{2j}.
\]
Using Parseval's identity and $h_2(x)=(x^2-1)/\sqrt2$, we obtain
\[
    \sum_{j\ge1}a_{2j}^2=\frac{1-p(K)}{p(K)},
    \qquad
    a_2^2=\frac{d(K)^2}{2}.
\]
The bounds \eqref{eq:Gaussian-Hermite-coarse} and \eqref{eq:Gaussian-Hermite-refined} now follow from $\log(1+x)\le x$. 

We next prove \eqref{eq:Gaussian-small-window}. We use the shorthands
\[
    P(\theta)=p^{(2)}(K,K,\theta),
    \qquad
    z=\frac{K^2\theta}{1-\theta^2}.
\]
The derivative identity \eqref{eq:energy_derivative} gives
\[
    P'(\theta)
      =\frac{2e^{-K^2/(1-\theta^2)}\sinh z}
             {\pi\sqrt{1-\theta^2}}.
\]
Define $R(\theta):=(1-\theta^2)P'(\theta)/\theta.$ Logarithmic differentiation gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:log-diff-R}
    \theta(1-\theta^2)\frac{R'(\theta)}{R(\theta)}
      =z(1+\theta^2)\coth z-2z\theta-1.
\end{equation}
For $0<K\le2$, we claim
\begin{equation}\label{eq:coth-scalar}
    z(1+\theta^2)\coth z-2z\theta
       \le1+e^{-K^2}\theta^2.
\end{equation}
If $z\le1$, use
$z\coth z\le1+z^2/3$, and set
$u=K^2/(1-\theta^2)=z/\theta$. The claim reduces to
\[
    1-e^{-u(1-\theta^2)}-2u
      +\frac{1+\theta^2}{3}u^2\le0.
\]
For $u\le3$, we have
$1-e^{-u(1-\theta^2)}\le u(1-\theta^2)$, so the left-hand side is at most $u(1-\theta^2) - 2u + (1+\theta^2)u^2 / 3 = u(1+\theta^2)(u/3-1)\leq 0$.  If $u>3$, the conditions
$z\le1$ and $K\le2$ give $u\le2+\sqrt5$, and then since $\theta^2 u^2 = z^2 \leq 1$, the left-hand side above is
at most $(u^2-6u+4)/3<0$.

If $z\ge1$, then we use the inequality $z(1+\theta^2)\coth z - 2z\theta \leq z(1-\theta)^2 + (1+\theta^2) e^{-z}$. To prove the claim it is thus enough to show
\[
    z(1-\theta)^2+(1+\theta^2)e^{-z}\le1.
\]
The left-hand side is convex in $z$, and since $K \leq 2$, we have $1\le z\le\frac{4\theta}{1-\theta^2}.$
Evaluation at these two endpoints proves the inequality for
$\theta\ge\sqrt5-2$, which is precisely the range in which the interval
for $z$ is nonempty.  This proves \eqref{eq:coth-scalar}.

Since $p(K)\le\sqrt{2/\pi}\,K$, we have
$d(K)^2\ge e^{-K^2}$. From \eqref{eq:log-diff-R} and 
\eqref{eq:coth-scalar}, we obtain
\[
    R'(\theta)\le d(K)^2P'(\theta).
\]
Also note that $R(0)=d(K)^2P(0)$.  Integrating first this inequality and then
\[
    \frac{P'(\theta)}{P(\theta)}
       \le d(K)^2\frac{\theta}{1-\theta^2}
\]
gives
\[
    \log\frac{P(\theta)}{P(0)}
       \le-\frac{d(K)^2}{2}\log(1-\theta^2),
\]
as required.
